period.years_by_month: November and December: 2024 and 2025 (November 2024 from the 21st); January to October: 2025 and 2026 (October 2026 to the 24th)

definition.words: rose by more than a fifth of its usual range within 3 hours
definition.usual_range: The Environment Agency's usual range for the gauge (typicalRangeLow to typicalRangeHigh on its stage scale, from the flood-monitoring API), the range the site's River level tile draws. `typical_low_m` and `typical_high_m` are the values the run used.
definition.hours: Whole hours when the gauge had a reading at most 24 hours old, published 1 hour before (as the site would have had it), and the site would have shown no word: the level not above its usual range and not already rising fast
definition.rise_hours: Of those hours, how many were followed within 3 hours by a reading more than a fifth of the usual range above the hour's reading
definition.rises: Runs of consecutive rise hours at the gauge: about one for each separate rise

display.rule: A month is shown only with at least 480 hours counted and readings in both of its years; otherwise the page says nothing for that month. Fixed on 6 November 2026 from the spread of hours counted, before any page line was written.

claim.public_wording: How often, in each calendar month from 21 November 2024 to 24 October 2026, an hour at this gauge was followed within 3 hours by a rise of more than a fifth of its usual range. History from the Environment Agency's archived readings, not a forecast of what the river will do.
not_claimed: a forecast or a warning of a rise
anything about swimming safety or water quality
the river's level now or at the swim spot
that a month with no rise recorded will have none
anything about months or years outside the period

limits: Two years at most behind each month: November and December are 2024 and 2025 (November 2024 from the 21st); January to October are 2025 and 2026 (October 2026 to the 24th). Two winters are not a climate.
The readings are the Environment Agency's archived 15-minute series (Hydrology API), checked and corrected after the fact, not what the live feed showed at the time.

Hours when the river was already high, or already rising fast as the site's River level tile says it, are not counted, nor hours with no reading at most 24 hours old (read 1 hour late, as the site would have had it).

A fifth of the usual range is a different rise in metres at each gauge, and a lock or weir reach can rise with the weir's setting rather than the river (Trowlock Island on the Thames: the record's 5.4% is the lock pair).
The gauge can be some way from the swim spot; the figure is the gauge's, not the spot's.
Not a forecast: the record's model using this history, radar and upstream gauges (C3) was not shown better than this history alone, and nothing here says what the river will do tomorrow.
